The representation ring is the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional complex unitary representations of a compact group, with addition induced by direct sum and multiplication by tensor product. Its invariant Laurent polynomials are the symmetric polynomials in xi​=zi​+zi−1​, hence the polynomial ring in their elementary symmetric polynomials e1​,…,em​. Restriction of the group representation ring of a compact group is injective because every group element is conjugate into the torus and characters distinguish virtual representations. For the defining complexified representation V, the exterior-power characters satisfy ∑k​χΛkV​tk=(1+t)∏i​(1+xi​t+t2). For k≤m, its coefficient is ek​ plus an integral linear combination of ej​ for j<k. Induction puts every ek​ in the restriction image, proving equality with the invariant ring and giving polynomial generators [Λ1V],…,[ΛmV].

An orthogonal representation is a real group representation preserving a positive-definite inner product, equivalently a group homomorphism into an orthogonal group. A representation over the rational numbers is a group representation on a finite-dimensional rational vector space. Choosing a basis gives rational matrices. Scalar extension yields representations over every characteristic-zero field.

If a representation has one-dimensional endomorphism algebra, it cannot be a direct sum of two nonzero invariant subspaces: the two coordinate projections would be independent endomorphisms. A two-dimensional representation of an abelian group fitting into an extension of two distinct linear characters splits. Choose an element on which the linear characters differ. The argument does not apply when the two linear characters coincide.

Geometric invariant theory constructs algebraic quotients of group actions by a reductive algebraic group using invariant sections and a chosen linearization of a line bundle. An affine quotient is the spectrum of the polynomial invariant ring; a projective quotient uses homogeneous invariants and excludes the points where all positive-degree invariants vanish. Group representation OurBigBook.com
The trivial representation sends every group element to the identity linear map.

Gauge singlet (R(g)=1)

Words: 75
Trivial representation OurBigBook.com
A field is a gauge singlet if it transforms in the trivial representation of the entire gauge group: every gauge transformation leaves it unchanged. A singlet of only one factor need not be a gauge singlet of the product group. For example a right-handed neutrino with representation (1,1)0​ is a Standard Model gauge singlet, whereas a color-singlet charged lepton is still acted on by the electroweak group. A singlet can have ordinary derivatives in its kinetic term and gauge-invariant masses, subject to Lorentz invariance and any additional global symmetries.

Scalar representation (1)

Words: 24
Trivial representation OurBigBook.com
A scalar representation is the one-dimensional trivial representation: every group element acts as the identity. Scalar polarization labels are unchanged by the relevant rotation group.

Vector representation

Words: 33
Group representation OurBigBook.com
The vector representation is the defining action of a matrix group on the vector space on which its matrices act. For an orthogonal or Lorentz group, it preserves the corresponding symmetric bilinear form.

Matrix representation

Words: 26
Group representation OurBigBook.com
A matrix representation is a group representation together with a basis, so each group element is represented by an invertible matrix and multiplication is represented by matrix multiplication.

Invariant subspace

Words: 87 Articles: 2
Group representation OurBigBook.com
An invariant subspace of a linear map A:V→V is a vector subspace W⊆V satisfying A(W)⊆W. For a group representation, invariance means ρ(g)W⊆W for every represented group element g.

Fixed-point subspace of a group action (Fix(H)={v:hv=v ∀h∈H})

Words: 41
Invariant subspace OurBigBook.com
For a linear group representation, the common fixed vectors of a subgroup form an invariant subspace for any equivariant map restricted to it. Its dimension is central to symmetry-based branching theorems. It need not be invariant under the entire group; conjugate subgroups have conjugate fixed-point subspaces.

Reducible representation

Words: 17
Invariant subspace OurBigBook.com
A nonzero representation is reducible when it has a nonzero proper invariant subspace; otherwise it is an irreducible representation.

Semisimple representation

Words: 20
Group representation OurBigBook.com
A representation is semisimple when it is a direct sum of irreducible representations. Equivalently, every invariant subspace has an invariant complement.

Maschke's theorem

Words: 42
Representation theory OurBigBook.com
Every group representation of a finite group over a field whose characteristic does not divide the number of elements of the group is semisimple. Given an invariant subspace, averaging any projection onto it over the group produces an equivariant projection, whose kernel is an invariant complement.

Words: 5k Articles: 89
Representation theory OurBigBook.com
Modular representation theory studies representations of a finite group G over a field whose characteristic divides ∣G∣. The group algebra is then generally nonsemisimple, and projective modules, radicals, blocks and vertices replace complete reducibility as central tools.

Words: 54
Modular representation theory OurBigBook.com
A p-local module here is a finite direct sum of induced representations from normalizers NG​(Q) of nontrivial p-subgroups Q. This usage includes induction from G itself when G normalizes such a subgroup. Green correspondence and induction on vertex order express every finite module, or lattice over a complete valuation ring, as a difference of p-local modules after adjoining projective modules.

Splitting p-modular system ((K,O,k))

Words: 64
Modular representation theory OurBigBook.com
Here O is a complete discrete valuation ring with fraction field K of characteristic zero and residue field k of characteristic p. The system is splitting for the finite group and its subgroups when their simple representations over K and k are absolutely irreducible. It permits ordinary and modular representation theory to be compared by reduction of lattices modulo the maximal ideal.

Modular representation ring (Rk​(G))

Words: 82
Modular representation theory OurBigBook.com
The modular representation ring is the Grothendieck group of finite-dimensional group representations, with relations [V]=[U]+[W] for every short exact sequence 0→U→V→W→0, and multiplication [V][W]=[V⊗k​W] using the tensor product of group representations. The Jordan–Hölder theorem makes the classes of simple modules a free integral basis. Tensoring over a field is exact, so this multiplication is well defined. When k is a splitting field for finite group representations, Brauer characters identify C⊗Z​Rk​(G) with the algebra of complex class functions on p-regular elements. The splitting hypothesis is essential: F2​C3​≅F2​×F4​ has two simple modules, although C3​ has three 2-regular conjugacy classes.

Brauer–Nesbitt theorem

Brauer character OurBigBook.com
The Brauer character of a finite-dimensional modular representation determines its semisimplification. More strongly, the irreducible Brauer characters are linearly independent as complex-valued functions on the p-regular conjugacy classes.
Brauer character basis theorem
Words: 139
Brauer–Nesbitt theorem OurBigBook.com
Over a splitting field for finite group representations of characteristic p, the irreducible Brauer characters form a complex basis of the class functions on the p-regular elements. Independence is the character form of the Brauer–Nesbitt theorem. To obtain spanning, extend such a class function by zero on the p-singular classes. Ordinary irreducible characters form a basis of all class functions by character orthogonality. Restricting them to p-regular elements yields Brauer characters of reductions of an integral form of a group representation in a compatible splitting p-modular system; if needed, first extend scalars, which does not change the simple-module list under the splitting hypothesis. Each restriction is a nonnegative integral sum of simple Brauer characters by exact-sequence additivity and the Jordan–Hölder theorem. Thus these restrictions span, proving the assertion. Consequently the number of simple modules equals the number of p-regular conjugacy classes, and evaluation identifies the complexified modular representation ring with the product of one copy of C for each such class.

A vertex of an indecomposable kG-module is a subgroup minimal among those for which the module is relatively projective. Vertices exist, form one conjugacy class, and are p-groups when k has characteristic p. The vertices of the trivial module are the Sylow p-subgroups.

Vertex of an indecomposable module OurBigBook.com
Every noncyclic finite finite p-group P has a quotient Cp​×Cp​. Over any field of characteristic p, define a square-zero representation with basis v0​,…,vr​,w1​,…,wr​ by xvi​=wi​ for 1≤i≤r, xv0​=0, yvi​=wi+1​ for 0≤i<r, yvr​=0, and xW=yW=0. Here x=g−1, y=h−1, and W is the span of the wi​. An endomorphism induces the same scalar on the top and on W; the remaining maps from the top to W form a square-zero ideal. Thus the endomorphism ring is local and the module is indecomposable. Inflating to P and choosing p∤2r+1 gives infinitely many distinct dimensions with vertex P: the trace of a relative-trace identity from any proper subgroup would force dimension zero in the field. Green correspondence OurBigBook.com
Let NG​(D)≤H≤G and let U be indecomposable with vertex D over H. The Mackey restriction formula writes ResHG​IndHG​U=U⊕T, where the vertices in T lie in H∩gD for g∈/H. Lifting inverse isomorphisms between reductions shows uniqueness among trivial source lattices.

Let k be an algebraically closed field and let a block of a group algebra B have a central defect group of a block D. Block with cyclic defect group
Words: 393 Articles: 4
Defect group of a block OurBigBook.com
A block has finite representation type exactly when its defect group is cyclic. In the forward implication, the block bimodule restricted to its defect group on both sides contains the regular defect-group bimodule as a summand; tensoring with arbitrary defect-group modules transfers finiteness to the defect group. Conversely, vertices are contained in the defect group and a cyclic p-group has only finitely many indecomposable modules, so there are only finitely many possible induced sources and their summands.
Brauer tree algebra
Words: 315 Articles: 3
Block with cyclic defect group OurBigBook.com
The basic algebra of a split block with cyclic defect is a Brauer tree algebra: its simple modules are indexed by the edges of a tree, with a distinguished vertex carrying the exceptional multiplicity. For a one-edge tree of multiplicity m, its basic algebra is k[t]/(tm+1). Its ideals form the chain of powers of t, so its unique indecomposable projective is uniserial of length m+1.
Uniserial branch of a Brauer tree algebra (1≤q≤mv​val(v))
Words: 93
Brauer tree algebra OurBigBook.com
Let i be an edge at v. Kill the other radical branch of its indecomposable projective module. The resulting uniserial module has length mv​val(v) and its factors follow the cyclic edge order beginning at i. Quotienting its radical powers gives all shorter such modules. The edge succession uniquely fixes the path, and its nonzero arrow maps can be rescaled to one, giving uniqueness up to isomorphism. At an exceptional leaf this reduces to a nilpotent single Jordan chain; the other leaf loop, when present, is a socle path and vanishes in these shorter quotients.
Brauer tree path presentation
Words: 113
Brauer tree algebra OurBigBook.com
Use a finite tree with cyclically ordered incident edges at each vertex, and multiplicities one except possibly at one vertex. Quiver vertices are tree edges; arrows follow each cyclic successor order, including loops at vertices of valency one. For an edge i with endpoints v,w, write Ci,v​ for the cycle around v. Impose Ci,vmv​​=Ci,wmw​​, Ci,vmv​​αi,v​=0, and zero for any path that switches from one vertex-cycle to the other. The quotient of this path algebra is the basic Brauer tree algebra; redundant valency-one loops can be eliminated. Its indecomposable projective at i has simple top and socle labelled by i, with two uniserial radical branches of lengths mv​val(v) and mw​val(w) meeting in that socle.

In characteristic 2, a Sylow subgroup P of A5​ is a Klein four-group, and its normalizer is A4​. Since kA4​ has one block, Brauer first main theorem gives a unique block of kA5​ with defect P. No order-two subgroup D can be a defect group of a block: both CA5​​(D) and CA5​​(P) equal P, so the Brauer morphisms of a central block idempotent at D and at P are equal. A nonzero image is 1, since a group algebra of a p-group in characteristic p is local, and consequently D is not maximal among subgroups with nonzero Brauer image.
Trace criterion for defect groups
Words: 194
Defect group of a block OurBigBook.com
For a p-subgroup D of a finite group G, set ID​=TrDG​((kG)D), a transfer ideal of conjugation-fixed elements in Z(kG). A block of a group algebra idempotent b lies in ID​ if and only if a defect group of a block of b is conjugate to a subgroup of D. In particular, defect groups can equivalently be defined as minimal subgroups D with b∈ID​.
Here is a proof using the Brauer morphism. A subgroup of smallest order with b∈ID​ exists, since a Sylow subgroup P gives b=TrPG​(b/[G:P]). Write b=TrDG​(a) and replace a by ba. If BrD​(b)=0, then ba belongs to the kernel of the Brauer morphism, which is the sum of proper-subgroup relative traces. Hence b∈∑Q<D​IQ​. The algebra bZ(kG) is a commutative Artinian ring and a local ring, so multiplying this equality by b forces some ideal bIQ​ to contain its identity b. This contradicts minimality. On the other hand, BrE​(ID​)=0 unless E is conjugate into D: the E-action on G/D has no fixed coset otherwise, and nonfixed orbit sizes vanish in characteristic p. Thus these minimal subgroups are precisely the maximal subgroups with nonzero Brauer image. They are all conjugate. Trace transitivity proves the stated criterion for larger D.

Brauer morphism OurBigBook.com
For a normal p-subgroup P◃G, every central idempotent e of kG satisfies e=BrP​(e)∈kCG​(P). Indeed a nonfixed conjugation orbit sum maps to zero in k(G/P), so e−BrP​(e) belongs to the nilpotent ideal J(kP)kG. Normality makes the Brauer image a central idempotent of kG, and two central idempotents congruent modulo a nilpotent ideal coincide. Consequently the blocks of a group algebra of kG correspond to G-orbits of blocks of kCG​(P).

Brauer morphism OurBigBook.com
For a p-subgroup P, the Brauer quotient removes all fixed vectors produced by proper-subgroup relative traces. On a permutation module it has a basis of the permutation-basis elements fixed by P: nonsingleton orbit sums are traces and disappear. The construction commutes with direct sums and idempotent projections. For an indecomposable trivial source module, it is nonzero exactly when a vertex contains a conjugate of P.

BrD​:ID​=TrDG​((kG)D)⟶JD​=TrDN​(kC)=(kC)DN​.

This follows from Brauer morphism and relative trace and the fact that kC is contained in (kG)D. The target is an ideal in the commutative algebra (kC)N. Brauer morphism OurBigBook.com
Let D be a p-subgroup of G, put N=NG​(D), and let k have characteristic p. The Brauer morphism intertwines the two relative traces:
BrD​(TrDG​(a))=TrDN​(BrD​(a))(a∈(kG)D).

Indeed, D acts on G/D by left multiplication. A coset gD is fixed exactly when g∈N, and every other orbit has size divisible by p. After applying BrD​, the summands belonging to one such orbit are equal, so every nonfixed orbit contributes zero in characteristic p; the fixed cosets give the trace from D to N.

Words: 163 Articles: 1
Brauer correspondence OurBigBook.com
Let b be a block of a group algebra of kH with defect group of a block D, where DCG​(D)≤H≤G. Apply Brauer first main theorem inside H to obtain its correspondent in NH​(D). Composing that correspondent's central character of a block with the Brauer morphism from Z(kG) selects a unique block of a group algebra bG. Block induction requires the block's defect centralizer
Words: 97
Block induction OurBigBook.com
The centralizer condition defining block induction refers to a defect group of a block of the actual source block. Containment of the centralizer of an unrelated p-subgroup does not suffice. For example, in characteristic 3 take G=A5​, H=A4​ and D=C3​. Then DCG​(D)≤H, but the unique defect-zero block of kA4​ occurs on bimodule restriction of both three-dimensional defect-zero blocks of kA5​. The two ordinary degree-three characters have identical restriction to A4​, namely its degree-three character, and defect-zero reduction gives the same simple projective module. Thus the unique-block characterization fails if D is not the defect group of the source block.

(Tp)(x)=p(x+1),(Sp)(x)=p(−x).
(74)
Then S2=I and STS=T−1. The operator T has one size-three unipotent Jordan block, so this three-dimensional representation cannot split into invariant subspaces of dimension at most two.

Induced two-dimensional dihedral representation

Representation of the infinite dihedral group OurBigBook.com
For λ=±1, the rotation acts by diag(λ,λ−1) and the reflection interchanges the two eigenlines.

One-dimensional character

Words: 48 Articles: 1
Representation theory OurBigBook.com
A one-dimensional character is a character of a representation arising from a one-dimensional representation, equivalently a homomorphism from a group to the multiplicative group of its scalar field.

One-dimensional characters factor through the abelianization

Words: 24
One-dimensional character OurBigBook.com
Every one-dimensional character kills the commutator subgroup and therefore factors through the abelianization. Conversely, every character of the abelianization pulls back to a one-dimensional character of the group.

Finite quotient representation

Words: 18
Representation theory OurBigBook.com
A representation factors through a finite quotient exactly when its kernel contains the defining kernel of that quotient.

Indecomposable representation

Words: 104 Articles: 3
Representation theory OurBigBook.com
An indecomposable representation is nonzero and cannot be expressed as a direct sum of two nonzero invariant subspaces. It is an indecomposable module over the associated group algebra or representing algebra.

Nonsplit extension of representations

Words: 63 Articles: 1
Indecomposable representation OurBigBook.com
A nonsplit extension contains an invariant subrepresentation with no invariant complementary subspace.

Split extension as a degeneration

Words: 51
Nonsplit extension of representations OurBigBook.com
An extension's vertexwise split arrow matrices are (fX​0​ξfZ​​). Scaling the subobject by t multiplies ξ by t. Nonzero t preserves the middle isomorphism class; t=0 gives X⊕Z. For a nonsplit extension, the split orbit is distinct and lies in the smaller-dimensional boundary of the middle orbit closure.

Unipotent representation

Words: 16
Indecomposable representation OurBigBook.com
A unipotent operator has every eigenvalue equal to one and may create a nonsplit Jordan-block extension.
